entities.name: Physical Deterioration
entities.description: Physical deterioration of carriers: mold, water damage, vinegar syndrome, magnetic-tape decay, and fragile newsprint destroying Black cultural materials, concentrated where storage is improvised and conservation staff absent.

claims.claim: Mold damage to African American Collection photographs at Emory University
claims.evidence: Emory Libraries' Preservation Office received photographic items from the Stuart A. Rose Manuscript, Archives, and Rare Book Library's African American Collection for mold treatment: sixteen studio prints, four tintypes, three ambrotypes, and two larger convex photographs. Mold covered the images due to moisture damage and inappropriate housing, growing between items and open plastic sleeves. Conservation staff cleaned, HEPA-vacuumed, and encapsulated the items; surface stains associated with mold deterioration remained on some pieces. Evidence: Institutional conservation blog with before/after treatment photographs documents moisture damage and inappropriate housing as the cause. Damage mechanism (mold between items and sleeves) is stated directly by the preservation staff.
claims.source: Emory Libraries, 'Rescuing Moldy Photographs' (Woodruff Libraries blog) — https://scholarblogs.emory.edu/woodruff/news/rescuing-moldy-photographs
claims.publication_date: Treatment documented circa 2019 (blog post; last crawl context); damage accumulated over an indeterminate prior period

claims.claim: Hurricane Katrina flood damage to the Calhoun–McCormick photographic archive (Black New Orleans)
claims.evidence: In 2005, documentary photographers Keith Calhoun and Chandra McCormick evacuated ahead of Hurricane Katrina, placing ~30 years of photographic work (film) in Rubbermaid bins on top of tables in their Lower Ninth Ward home/studio. They returned to toppled bins and waterlogged negatives: decades documenting Black New Orleanians — second-line parades, the prison industrial complex, everyday joy and struggle — were flood-damaged. Evidence: National Geographic (2021) interview with the photographers directly quoting their account of the bins, the waterlogging, and the loss. Partial salvage/restoration followed; the event is presented as personal/collective loss, not total destruction — some material was salvaged and exhibited.
claims.source: National Geographic, 'Warped and Waterlogged, a Damaged Photo Collection Takes on New Life' (2021) — https://www.nationalgeographic.com/photography/article/warped-and-waterlogged-a-damaged-photo-collection-takes-on-new-life

claims.claim: HBCU radio broadcast tapes deteriorating beyond repair
claims.evidence: Radio producer Jocelyn Robinson's survey of HBCU radio station archives (NPR, Feb 2020) found cassette tapes and floppy disks thrown into unlabeled boxes or bags and reel-to-reel tape 'past repair' at some schools; at one school, nothing was saved from over 40 years of broadcasting. The Northeast Document Conservation Center's HBCU Radio Preservation Project (Mellon-funded, 2026 field reporting) confirms that broadcasts documenting campus life, local communities, music, news, and the Black experience survive on deteriorating audio formats. Evidence: NPR reporting (WUOT/WEKU, Feb 16, 2020) quoting Robinson directly with specific examples; NEDCC field archivist reporting (Aug 20, 2026) describing format-by-format deterioration. Both are institutional/press sources with named staff. Some tapes are already irrecoverable — extent across all HBCUs is not quantified in these sources (gap noted).
claims.source: NPR/WUOT, 'One Woman's Quest To Preserve The Radio Archives At Historically Black Colleges' (Feb 16, 2020) — https://www.wuot.org/2020-02-16/one-womans-quest-to-preserve-the-radio-archives-at-historically-black-colleges
claims.publication_date: Surveys 2019–2026; materials date from the 1960s onward

entities.name: Institutional Closure
entities.description: Closure (or near-closure) of the Black-led institution holding a collection, converting archives into bankruptcy assets, dispersed property, or unfunded orphans.

claims.claim: Johnson Publishing Company bankruptcy and closure (Chicago) — archive endangered
claims.evidence: Chicago-based Johnson Publishing Company, publisher of Ebony (founded 1945) and Jet (founded 1951), filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy on April 9, 2019, owing $13.6 million to Capital V Holdings (controlled by George Lucas and Mellody Hobson). Its archive — 4–4.5 million prints and negatives, ~10,000 audio/visual recordings, thousands of hours of video footage, and business records — was put up for auction July 2019 to pay creditors. There was extended public anxiety the archive would be won by private collectors and closed to research. A consortium of four foundations (Ford, J. Paul Getty Trust, MacArthur, Mellon) purchased it for just under $30 million and donated it to the Smithsonian NMAAHC and the Getty Research Institute. Evidence: Multiple corroborating outlets (Hyperallergic, CJR, Smithsonian Magazine, NPR/KHSU, Hilco Streambank's own sale announcement via ABL Advisor) agree on bankruptcy date, creditor, auction timing, price, and buyers. Outcome (preservation) is confirmed; the risk phase (auction jeopardy) is documented contemporaneously. Note: the collection was appraised at $46–47 million in 2015 (Hyperallergic/CNN) but sold for ~$30M.
claims.source: Hyperallergic, 'An Essential History Immortalized in the Archive of Ebony and Jet' (2019) — https://hyperallergic.com/ebony-and-jet-archive-sale/

claims.claim: America's Black Holocaust Museum (Milwaukee) closed 2008; reopened as virtual museum 2012
claims.evidence: The Black Holocaust Museum in Milwaukee, founded by lynching survivor James Cameron as a memorial to enslavement, closed in 2008 due to financial difficulties. It reopened in 2012 as a virtual museum; its physical collection's disposition during the closure is the risk event. (A physical museum later reopened in Milwaukee in 2022 — outside the scope of the closure event itself.) Evidence: Hyperallergic's 'Resting in Pieces: The Scattered Fate of Closed Museums' documents the 2008 closure and 2012 virtual reopening. Single-source for this entry; corroboration not obtained in this research pass — flagged as a follow-up.
claims.source: Hyperallergic, 'Resting in Pieces: The Scattered Fate of Closed Museums' — https://hyperallergic.com/resting-in-pieces-the-scattered-fate-of-closed-museums/

claims.claim: WDCU radio license sold by University of the District of Columbia during financial crisis
claims.evidence: The University of the District of Columbia — an HBCU — sold its radio station WDCU's broadcast license for $13 million to C-SPAN during a financial crisis (reported by NPR in Feb 2020 as 'twenty-three years ago,' i.e., ~1997), eliminating the station as a going concern. Curator Judith Korey and colleagues physically carried over what they could: ~14,000 recordings (LPs, CDs, cassettes, tapes), business records, membership lists, program guides, photographs. What could not be carried over was lost. Evidence: NPR (WUOT/WEKU) reporting with named sources (Jocelyn Robinson, Judith Korey) and specific figures ($13M, 14,000 recordings). Date is derived ('twenty-three years ago' from Feb 2020), not stated as a calendar year — noted as an approximation.
claims.source: NPR/WUOT, 'One Woman's Quest To Preserve The Radio Archives At Historically Black Colleges' (Feb 16, 2020) — https://www.wuot.org/2020-02-16/one-womans-quest-to-preserve-the-radio-archives-at-historically-black-colleges
claims.uncertainty: Red-team re-audit 2026-09-28 (Provisional): Single source (NPR/WUOT, Feb 2020); FCC-record corroboration exists under E-091 but is not cited here.

claims.claim: Moorland-Spingarn Research Center closure scare (Howard University, 2009) — threatened but did not close
claims.evidence: In November 2009, Howard University's student newspaper reported that the Moorland-Spingarn Research Center — described as one of the foremost repositories of artifacts and manuscripts related to Black history — could close due to inadequate budget and staff shortages. The report prompted national outcry (including The Root). Howard's associate provost stated the university had no plans to close the center, and retiring director Thomas C. Battle said his comments had been misinterpreted and he did not believe it would close. Battle did confirm chronic trouble: staff cut by more than half since the early 1990s (an ~80% personnel reduction over 15 years), only 10 staff remaining, inadequate storage and processing space. Evidence: Inside Higher Ed contemporaneous reporting (Nov 11, 2009) with on-the-record statements from Battle and Howard's associate provost. This is a documented closure THREAT, not a closure — recorded here as evidence of the risk mechanism, not as a loss.
claims.source: Inside Higher Ed, 'Black History At Risk?' (Nov 11, 2009) — https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2009/11/11/black-history-risk
claims.uncertainty: Red-team re-audit 2026-09-28 (Provisional): Single source (Inside Higher Ed, Nov 2009) for the closure scare and the ~80% staff-reduction figure.

entities.name: Building Demolition
entities.description: Demolition of a building destroying the records inside it. No documented case found in this research pass - recorded as an explicit negative finding; uncataloged materials destroyed in demolitions would leave no paper trail.

claims.claim: No documented case found
claims.evidence: No documented case was found in this research pass of a building demolition that destroyed Black archival records or collections. Adjacent documented losses exist: (a) the 1921 fire that destroyed most of the 1890 U.S. Census, creating a lasting documentation gap for descendants of formerly enslaved people (the census is the only federal enumeration of the post-emancipation generation); and (b) documented demolition of Black historic sites, e.g., dozens of Black historic sites demolished in Wilmington, NC (Beacon Journal, 2022), and the 1857 demolition of Seneca Village, the predominantly Black community razed for Central Park. These are site/building losses, not records-destruction-by-demolition. Evidence: Two rounds of targeted web searches (Sept 2026) returned no case of demolition destroying Black records. Adjacent cases cited are from secondary sources. This gap is a candidate for deeper archival/oral-history research.
claims.source: Beacon Journal, 'Preserving Black history: Why dozens of Black historic sites are gone in Wilmington' (Feb 2022) — https://www.beaconjournal.com/story/news/2022/02/21/preserving-black-history-why-dozens-black-historic-sites-gone-wilmington/6721916001/
claims.uncertainty: No documented case found in this research pass; recorded as an explicit negative finding.

entities.name: Ownership Change
entities.description: Ownership or control changes - bankruptcy sales, corporate acquisitions, strategy pivots - that endanger or erase Black cultural holdings. Corporate-held Black memory is revocable memory.

claims.claim: BET Digital written archive deleted after Paramount Skydance ownership change (2026)
claims.evidence: Following Paramount's ownership of BET (the company using the Paramount Skydance name at the time of the deletion), BET Digital permanently removed its entire written news archive from BET.com in early September 2026 as part of a 'video-first pivot,' without warning. Years of Black journalism, cultural critique, and political reporting vanished from the live web; many writers lost their only record of their work. The Internet Archive had preserved 199,000+ BET articles and released a searchable pilot explorer (wayback-labs.sf.archive.org/bet-explorer/) on September 8, 2026. Evidence: HuffPost (first report, via Phil Lewis) quoted by multiple outlets; Black Enterprise (Sept 9, 2026, Selena Hill) confirms; infoDOCKET documents the Internet Archive's 199,000-article rescue and explorer launch. Floyd Webb's Substack essay (a Chicago filmmaker, secondary commentary) notes the contrast: Jet's archive was sold for $30M and preserved; BET's was deleted. Corroborated across four outlets — deletion itself is not disputed; framing ('digital gentrification') is commentary.
claims.source: Black Enterprise, 'Years Of Black Journalism Disappeared From BET\u2019s Website' (Sept 9, 2026) — https://www.blackenterprise.com/years-of-black-journalism-disappeared-bet-digital/

claims.claim: MTV News archive wiped under Paramount ownership (2024)
claims.evidence: In June 2024, Paramount scrubbed the MTV News website, deleting over two decades of music and pop-culture journalism to avoid web-server and maintenance costs. The archive included extensive coverage of hip-hop and Black popular music. Evidence: Reported by The A.V. Club and referenced in infoDOCKET and TheHub.news coverage of the BET deletion. This entry relies on secondhand references in the BET coverage; the original A.V. Club report was not directly fetched — flagged for follow-up verification.

claims.claim: Johnson Publishing Company archive bankruptcy auction (2019) — see institutional_closure entry
claims.evidence: Cross-reference: the JPC bankruptcy auction (July 2019, ~$30M sale to Ford/Getty/MacArthur/Mellon consortium, donation to NMAAHC and Getty Research Institute) is both an institutional closure and an ownership-change risk event. Full detail recorded under institutional_closure. Evidence: See institutional_closure entry.
claims.source: See institutional_closure entry: Johnson Publishing Company bankruptcy and closure (Chicago)

entities.name: Obsolete Formats
entities.description: Carriers whose playback and migration paths are disappearing: reel-to-reel and cassette tape, U-matic and half-inch video, floppy disks, unlabeled CDs, MiniDV/DAT with dead transfer software.

claims.claim: HBCU radio archives stranded on reel-to-reel, cassette, and floppy disk
claims.evidence: See physical_deterioration entry. The same evidence documents the format dimension: HBCU broadcasts survive on reel-to-reel tape, cassettes, floppy disks, and unlabeled CDs — formats whose playback equipment is disappearing and whose media is chemically degrading. The NEDCC's 2026 field report details the specific carriers (open-reel, cassette, DAT-era media) and their failure modes. Evidence: NEDCC field archivist reporting (Aug 2026); NPR (Feb 2020).
claims.source: NEDCC, '40 Years of HBCU Radio Broadcast Formats' (Aug 20, 2026) — https://www.nedcc.org/about/nedcc-stories/hbcu-formats

claims.claim: Chicago 'guerrilla television' tapes: half-inch open reel and U-matic endangered (UChicago)
claims.evidence: A UChicago Library project (reported ~2025) is digitizing the archive of the 1960s–70s guerrilla television movement, including videotapes documenting the lives of Black and Latinx youth and community issues. The project prioritizes 'highly endangered half-inch open reel and U-matics' — first- and second-generation 1970s videotapes. Technicians must repair physically broken tapes and sometimes bake them to remove moisture before real-time digitization. Evidence: UChicago News institutional reporting quoting project faculty (James Chandler) and describing the technical workflow. Chicago-anchored.
claims.source: UChicago News, 'The hidden history of guerrilla television: UChicago scholars preserve decades-old videos' — http://news.uchicago.edu/story/hidden-history-guerrilla-television-uchicago-scholars-preserve-decades-old-videos

claims.claim: Johnson Publishing archive: ~10,000 audio/visual recordings on legacy media
claims.evidence: The JPC archive included roughly 10,000 audio and visual recordings (HNN) / 'several thousand hours of video footage' (CNN via EURweb), plus 200 boxes of business records and 4.5M prints/negatives — much of it on legacy formats. At the time of the 2019 sale, 'very few' of the photographs had been digitized (CNN via EURweb), implying the A/V holdings were largely inaccessible on original carriers. Evidence: HNN digitization-progress article and CNN/EURweb sale reporting give the counts; 'very few digitized' is from CNN via EURweb. Exact format breakdown (how much is U-matic, VHS, 16mm, etc.) is not public in these sources — gap noted.
claims.source: History News Network, 'Progress Digitizing the Johnson Publishing Archive' — https://www.hnn.us/article/progress-digitizing-the-johnson-publishing-archive

entities.name: Website Disappearance
entities.description: Deliberate or negligent removal of Black cultural content from the live web by its operator, with no warning or export path.

claims.claim: BET Digital written archive deleted (September 2026)
claims.evidence: Cross-reference: full detail under ownership_change. BET Digital permanently removed its entire written news archive from the live web in September 2026 ('video-first pivot'); Internet Archive preserved 199,000+ articles via Wayback Machine and a pilot explorer. Evidence: Corroborated by HuffPost (first report), Black Enterprise, infoDOCKET, TheHub.news.
claims.source: See ownership_change entry: BET Digital written archive deleted (2026)

claims.claim: MTV News archive deleted (June 2024)
claims.evidence: Cross-reference: full detail under ownership_change. Paramount deleted the MTV News website's 20+ year archive. Evidence: Secondhand via infoDOCKET citing A.V. Club; original report not directly fetched.
claims.source: See ownership_change entry: MTV News archive wiped (2024)

entities.name: Domain Expiration
entities.description: Loss of Black cultural-memory content through domain expiry. No documented case found in this research pass - recorded as an explicit negative finding; the exposure surface (small archives, personal sites, no IT staff) is real.

claims.claim: No documented case found
claims.evidence: No documented case was found in this research pass of a Black cultural-memory website losing its content because its domain expired. The closest adjacent case: the NAACP accidentally allowed defensive domains (nigger.com/.org/.net, held ~20 years to keep them from hate groups) to expire; they went to a NameJet auction (72 bids, $10,000 high bid) before the NAACP reclaimed them (Domain Incite, ~2017). No cultural-memory content was lost in that incident — the risk was reputational/hijack, and the domains were recovered. Evidence: Two rounds of targeted searches returned no Black cultural-memory domain-expiration loss. The NAACP incident is documented by Domain Incite. This remains an open research gap.
claims.source: Domain Incite, 'Nigger.com returned to NAACP after expiration prompts $10,000 auction' — https://domainincite.com/21537-nigger-com-returned-to-naacp-after-expiration-prompts-10000-auction
claims.publication_date: Research pass completed September 2026; adjacent incident ~2017
claims.uncertainty: No documented case found in this research pass; recorded as an explicit negative finding.

entities.name: Platform Shutdown
entities.description: Shutdowns, migrations, or policy purges on commercial platforms destroying user-uploaded Black cultural content with no preservation contract.

claims.claim: MySpace server migration deleted 50M+ songs (2003–2015 uploads), including early Black artists' work
claims.evidence: In March 2019 MySpace disclosed that a server migration had deleted 'any photos, videos, and audio files you uploaded more than three years ago' — over 50 million songs uploaded between 2003 and 2015, from ~14 million artists (The Guardian via NPR/MTPR; Advanced Television). MySpace called it an accident; critics (e.g., Andy Baio) publicly doubted that. The Internet Archive later hosted ~450,000 recovered MP3s (the 'MySpace Music Dragon Hoard,' collected 2008–2010 by an academic group studying music networks) — under 1% of the estimated loss. Evidence: NPR/MTPR (March 18, 2019) and Advanced Television report the 50M/14M figures; TechCrunch (April 3, 2019) documents the 450K-song partial recovery and names recovered Black artists. Whether the deletion was accidental or a cost-cutting measure is disputed — both positions are on record; the fact of the loss is not.
claims.source: NPR/MTPR, 'MySpace Says It Lost Years Of User-Uploaded Music' (Mar 18, 2019) — https://www.mtpr.org/2019-03-18/myspace-says-it-lost-years-of-user-uploaded-music

claims.claim: Vine shutdown (2017) — Black creator culture stranded
claims.evidence: Twitter shut down the Vine app in January 2017. Vine had been a major platform for Black comedic and creative expression ('Black Vine' was a recognized cultural phenomenon). Twitter kept the Vine archive viewable online for a time, then took the full Vine archive offline in 2019. This entry is included as a Provisional case: the cultural significance is well documented, but this research pass did not verify the specifics of what was lost versus preserved from a Black-cultural-memory standpoint. Evidence: Shutdown dates are widely reported; the Black-cultural-memory loss dimension was not sourced to a specific citation in this pass — flagged as needing verification before being treated as more than Provisional.

entities.name: Poor Metadata
entities.description: Unprocessed and underprocessed backlogs, orphaned context, and thin description that make saved Black collections unfindable, unusable, and undefendable - the stage where the chain breaks worst by the numbers.

claims.claim: BMRC Survey Initiative (2009–2011): Chicago Black collections unprocessed and inaccessible
claims.evidence: The Black Metropolis Research Consortium's Mellon-funded Survey Initiative (2009–2011) identified and assessed 'irreplaceable primary resources of African American and African related archival materials' across Chicago. Although the survey revealed 'a treasure trove of previously unknown historical material,' UChicago News reports that 'many collections weren't processed or accessible to the public' — i.e., they existed in backlogs without finding aids or catalog records. The BMRC responded with the Color Curtain Processing Project and, later, a cross-institutional Archives Portal. Evidence: BMRC's own program pages (bmrc.lib.uchicago.edu) describe the survey methodology and goals; UChicago News (institutional) states the 'weren't processed or accessible' finding; the BMRC exhibit text (lib.uchicago.edu PDF) describes initial studies of backlogs in processing Black historical collections. Chicago-anchored, multi-source, consistent.

claims.claim: 'Hidden collections': hundreds of linear feet of Black history uncataloged in secure shelving
claims.evidence: A Bunk History essay by an archivist describes 'hundreds of linear feet of Black history... stacked in secure shelving, unbeknownst and inaccessible to implicated communities,' including single-box collections titled 'Miscellaneous Slavery Documents' (Freedmen's Bureau papers and bills of sale encountered without meaningful description). The essay argues institutions respond by prioritizing digitization-as-images 'without full description or detailed metadata, the things that guide digital discovery.' Evidence: Single-source practitioner essay; the specific encounters ('Miscellaneous Slavery Documents') are anecdotal and the author's identity/institution were not captured in this pass. Treat as Provisional pending identification of the essay's provenance.
claims.publication_date: Essay published circa 2024–2026 (exact date not captured)

claims.claim: NHPRC/Shift Collective survey (2020): small and diverse archives face discovery and sustainability gaps
claims.evidence: The National Historical Publications and Records Commission funded Shift Collective to survey small and diverse archives (community-based archives, historical societies, HBCUs, tribal libraries, public libraries, civic/activist groups) in 2020 on funding, collections discovery, access, use, and long-term sustainability. The published report documents systemic under-resourcing of the institutions most likely to hold Black community records. Evidence: Primary report PDF from Shift Collective (hosted on Squarespace). Findings are survey-based; specific percentages were not extracted in this pass — follow-up should pull the numbers.
claims.source: Shift Collective, 'Needs Assessment to Identify Hidden Collections Documenting America's Diverse Culture and History' (report to NHPRC, 2021) — https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5f077037c9ef6a2f026bdd70/t/6068f6de78b53070e6d3d913/1617491685095/Shift-NHPRC+survey+report-2021.pdf

claims.claim: Teenie Harris archive: ~80,000 negatives largely untitled and undated
claims.evidence: When Carnegie Museum of Art acquired Charles 'Teenie' Harris's archive in 2001, few of his negatives were titled or dated. The museum has since run a years-long public-identification project (displays, oral historians, online response forms, NEH 'We the People' designation in 2007) to supply the missing metadata for 70,000+ images. Evidence: Carnegie Museum of Art's own archive pages and the Crowley Company preservation case study both state the negatives were untitled/undated at acquisition; the public-identification program is documented by CMOA and the Pittsburgh History & Landmarks Foundation (NEH grant reporting).
claims.source: Carnegie Museum of Art, 'About the Charles Teenie Harris Archive' (via stores.carnegiemuseums.org) — https://stores.carnegiemuseums.org/carnegie-museum-of-art/current-exhibitions/charles-teenie-harris-in-sharp-focus-/?price_min=0&price_max=14&sort=featured

entities.name: Unknown Ownership
entities.description: Orphan collections and found materials whose makers, subjects, provenance, or legal owners are unknown - blocking cataloging, digitization, and access decisions.

claims.claim: The Baltimore Collection: 53 'found' photographs of Black sitters, makers unknown
claims.evidence: In 2001, fifty-three photographs predominantly featuring Black sitters, obtained in Maryland, were donated to the University of Delaware Library as 'found objects' — no photographers, sitters, dates, or provenance known. They became 'The Baltimore Collection.' University seminars (2017, 2021, 2023) have since researched the objects to build metadata, grappling with 'the archival and theoretical challenges' of making such collections public, including biases in classification. Evidence: University of Delaware Library's Baltimore Collection project pages document the 'found objects' provenance and the seminar-based metadata-building effort.
claims.source: University of Delaware Library, 'Curating Hidden Collections & the Black Archive: Project Seminar | The Baltimore Collection' — https://sites.udel.edu/baltimorecollection/curating-hidden-collections-the-black-archive/

claims.claim: Teenie Harris negatives: decades of images with unknown subjects (ownership secured, context orphaned)
claims.evidence: Cross-reference: see poor_metadata entry. Ownership of the physical archive was secured by Carnegie Museum of Art (purchase from the Harris family, 2001), but the intellectual context — who is pictured, where, when — was orphaned. The museum's ongoing public-identification program is effectively an orphan-works rescue operation. Evidence: CMOA archive pages; PHLF grant reporting.
claims.source: See poor_metadata entry: Teenie Harris archive

claims.claim: Shorefront Legacy Center (Evanston, IL): rescuing orphaned Black suburban records from a church basement
claims.evidence: The Shorefront Legacy Center, a small archive in the basement of Evanston's historic Black Lula B. Sherman Church, has spent ~30 years collecting records of Black life in Chicago's northern suburbs — boxes of papers, photos, news clippings, local NAACP minutes, letters documenting segregation. NPR (Sept 19, 2026) reports the archive is 'filled from the floor to almost the ceiling' with materials that would otherwise be orphaned in attics, basements, and closing organizations. Its records were used to document Evanston's history of racial discrimination, supporting the city's 2021 reparations program. Evidence: NPR/KRPS reporting (Sept 19, 2026) with on-site reporting and quotes from archivist Laurice Bell. Chicago-anchored.
claims.source: NPR/KRPS, 'How Shorefront Legacy Center saves Black history from a church basement in Evanston' (Sept 19, 2026) — https://www.krps.org/2026-09-19/how-shorefront-legacy-center-saves-black-history-from-a-church-basement-in-evanston
claims.uncertainty: Red-team re-audit 2026-09-28 (Provisional): Single source (NPR/KRPS, Sept 2026); no second independent outlet cited.

entities.name: Copyright Uncertainty
entities.description: Orphan works, expired licenses, and adverse precedent chilling digitization, publication, and classroom use of Black historical materials.

claims.claim: Orphan works chill digitization of Black historical collections — Duke University Libraries filing to the Copyright Office (2013)
claims.evidence: In comments to the U.S. Copyright Office's 2012 Notice of Inquiry on orphan works and mass digitization, Duke University Libraries stated that its online digital collections 'undoubtedly contain orphan works,' specifically naming 'a collection of images from articles and advertising of mainline Protestant children and families, and another that documents African-American life in the Jim Crow South.' Duke described facing 'this uncertain situation every time we consider a digitization' decision, because rightsholders cannot be found and infringement liability (up to $150,000 per work) deters institutions from digitizing or publishing such materials. Evidence: Primary source: Duke's filed comments (PDF on copyright.gov) name the African-American-life collection explicitly and describe the chilling effect on digitization decisions. The Copyright Office's later recommendation (pay 'reasonable compensation' if owners surface) did not resolve the deterrent, per Chronicle reporting.
claims.source: Duke University Libraries, Comments in response to Copyright Office Notice of Inquiry on Orphan Works and Mass Digitization (Jan 2013) — https://www.copyright.gov/orphan/comments/noi_10222012/Duke-University-Libraries.pdf

claims.claim: Hachette v. Internet Archive (2023): precedent discouraging controlled digital lending of orphan works
claims.evidence: The Second Circuit unanimously affirmed (2023) that the Internet Archive's controlled digital lending — scanning print books in full and lending digital copies — was not fair use. Library Journal noted the ruling 'may set a discouraging precedent' for controlled digital lending, 'particularly as a way to preserve and circulate orphan works (for which the copyright holders are unknown) or books that are still under copyright but unlikely to ever be offered digitally.' Evidence: Library Journal's legal reporting quotes the unanimous panel. The connection to Black collections specifically is inferential (the ruling is content-neutral) — noted as such; the orphan-works link is stated in the source.
claims.source: Library Journal, 'Internet Archive Loses Appeal in Copyright Case' — https://www.libraryjournal.com/story/Book+News/internet-archive-loses-appeal-in-copyright-case
claims.publication_date: District ruling 2023; appeal affirmed (reported by Library Journal)

entities.name: Lack Of Digitization
entities.description: Analog-only or inaccessible holdings: rescued collections still hostage to a single physical location, years or decades behind digitization.

claims.claim: Johnson Publishing archive: 'very few' of 4M+ images digitized at time of 2019 sale
claims.evidence: At the July 2019 bankruptcy auction, reporting (CNN via EURweb) noted that of the archive's ~1 million printed images, 3 million negatives/contact sheets, and thousands of hours of video, 'very few have been digitized.' The Getty Trust subsequently committed $30 million to the organization and digitization of the archive; HNN later reported digitization progress from the Chicago warehouse. Evidence: CNN via EURweb contemporaneous reporting ('very few have been digitized'); Hyperallergic on the Getty's $30M digitization commitment; HNN on digitization progress. Consistent across sources.
claims.source: EURweb, 'Ebony and Jet Magazine\u2019s Photo Archives Auctioned Off in Private Sale' (2019) — https://eurweb.com/ebony-and-jet-magazines-photo-archives-auctioned-off-in-private-sale/

claims.claim: Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection: 300,000 pieces in-person-only until 2024 Mellon grant (Chicago)
claims.evidence: The Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection at Chicago Public Library's Woodson Regional Library — 'the largest cache of African American history and literature in the midwestern United States' — was historically available only for in-person viewing. In February 2024 the Mellon Foundation awarded CPL $2 million to digitize 300,000 pieces, with full digitization expected within three years. Evidence: Journal of Blacks in Higher Education reporting on the Mellon grant with the 300,000-piece figure and 'only available in person' history. Chicago-anchored.
claims.source: The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education, 'Chicago Library Receives $2 Million to Digitize Collection of African American History and Literature' (Feb 2024) — https://jbhe.com/2024/02/chicago-library-receives-2-million-to-digitize-collection-of-african-american-history-and-literature/
claims.publication_date: Collection built from 1932 onward; digitization grant February 2024
claims.uncertainty: Red-team re-audit 2026-09-28 (Provisional): Single source (JBHE, Feb 2024); the Mellon grant announcement itself is not cited as institutional evidence.

claims.claim: Obsidian Collection: Black press photo legacy effectively invisible online
claims.evidence: Chicagoan Angela Ford founded the Obsidian Collection Archives (2015) after discovering she could not find online any images of her grandmother — a Bronzeville businesswoman covered extensively by the Chicago Defender — via Google or other search engines. 'Digital dead-ends became a pattern whenever Ford sought images to illustrate black history.' The nonprofit now digitizes images from the Defender, Baltimore Afro-American, and 15+ other Black newspapers, partnering with Google Arts & Culture. entities.name: Collector Death

claims.claim: Teenie Harris dies (1998); ~80,000-negative archive sold by family to Carnegie Museum of Art (2001)
claims.evidence: Charles 'Teenie' Harris (1908–1998), Pittsburgh Courier photographer and one of the most prolific Black photographers of the 20th century, died of a heart attack on June 12, 1998, just shy of his 90th birthday. In 2001, Carnegie Museum of Art acquired the full archive — nearly 80,000 photographic negatives spanning ~1935–1975 — from the Harris family, 'honoring Harris' longstanding wish,' and began a multiyear preservation/cataloguing/digitization project (70,000+ images digitized; 75,000+ viewable online). Evidence: Crowley Company preservation case study (working from CMOA sources) gives the death date and acquisition narrative; CMOA's archive pages confirm the purchase from the family and the scale (70,000+ images). Multiple corroborating institutional sources.
claims.source: The Crowley Company, 'Accessing the Archive: Charles Teenie Harris and the Power of Preservation' (case study) — https://thecrowleycompany.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/CMOA-Accessing-the-Archive-Charles-Teenie-Harris-and-the-Power-of-Preservation_04_Interactive.pdf

claims.claim: John Hope Franklin estate sale disperses personal library (2017)
claims.evidence: Historian John Hope Franklin (1915–2009), the scholar of African American history whose work reshaped how the world thinks about slavery, died in 2009. In February 2017, an estate sale at his Durham, NC home dispersed thousands of books (hundreds on slavery, the South, Civil War, and Reconstruction — his specialty), signed volumes (including a book inscribed to Franklin by Rosa Parks's and MLK's attorney Fred Gray), awards, and household effects to the general public. NPR's report notes the bittersweet reaction of attendees who felt some items 'should belong in a museum.' Evidence: NPR (WUNC, Feb 27, 2017, via NPR Illinois) on-the-scene reporting with named attendees and specific items. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: the report covers the estate sale of household effects and books; it does not state where Franklin's scholarly papers went (widely reported elsewhere as Duke University, donated before his death — not verified in this research pass). This entry therefore documents dispersal of the personal collection, not loss of the core papers — graded Provisional on the scope of what was lost.
claims.source: NPR Illinois/WUNC, 'Estate Sale-Goers Discover Treasures In Home Of Historian John Hope Franklin' (Feb 27, 2017) — https://www.nprillinois.org/2017-02-27/estate-sale-goers-discover-treasures-in-home-of-historian-john-hope-franklin

entities.name: Lost Organizational Records
entities.description: Organizational records destroyed by state action (raids, seizures), disaster, or dissolution - leaving movements with no centralized archive.

claims.claim: Black Panther Party: no centralized archive; records seized and destroyed in raids
claims.evidence: The Black Panther Party (founded 1966, dissolved early 1980s) left no centralized institutional archive. Former Panther Billy Jennings (Daily Nebraskan) stated: 'party members are dying every year, and there is no archive for all the great work the movement had done,' prompting his personal collecting effort (now ~2,000 underground newspapers in his home). Separately, historian Ward Churchill documents that police/FBI raids 'cleaned out' Panther offices — 'furniture, bedding, clothing, file cabinets, party records' — in Denver, Indianapolis, Des Moines, San Francisco, New Bedford, Toledo, New Orleans, and Detroit (1968–1970), a pattern of seizure and destruction of the Party's own records. FBI wiretap tapes relevant to the Geronimo ji-Jaga (Pratt) case were also claimed destroyed by the FBI. Evidence: Churchill's documented raid accounts (hosted PDF of academic work; cites case-by-case sources); Jennings's direct quote in the Daily Nebraskan; Flint Taylor/In These Times on the FBI's 200-volume BPP file production in the Hampton/Clark litigation (showing the state's archive dwarfs the movement's). The Churchill source's hosting site (a band website) is non-ideal provenance — the underlying work is academic; flagged for stronger citation in follow-up.

claims.publication_date: Raids 1968–1970; party dissolved early 1980s; Jennings collecting from mid-1990s

claims.claim: Hurricane flooding destroyed FBI files on the National Negro Labor Council and Chicago's Claude Lightfoot

Also lost: 1/5 to 1/3 of the 62,000-page Birmingham file on the United Klans of America. Evidence: Gizmodo (2014) reporting Trevor Griffey's National Security Archive blog post, which was based on the FBI's FOIA response. The specific volume/page counts come from that reporting. The underlying FOIA response was not directly reviewed in this pass — the chain is FOIA → NSA blog → Gizmodo.
claims.source: Gizmodo, 'Thousands Of FBI Documents About Civil Rights Era Destroyed By Flooding' (2014) — https://gizmodo.com/thousands-of-fbi-documents-about-civil-rights-era-destr-1635448055
